Catabolism
Eicosanoids have a very short half-life, degrading very rapidly once they have been synthesized. In general, inactivation takes place
in a ﬁrst phase by the action of speciﬁc enzymes, which act very rapidly on the various types of eicosanoids. In a second, slower
phase, the metabolites resulting from the ﬁrst inactivation continue their catabolism by non-speciﬁc enzymes, some of which
are those that usually act in the degradation of fatty acids (b-oxidation system). The main site of eicosanoid catabolism is the
lung (Yonker et al., 2021).
Biological effects
As noted above, eicosanoids have a very short half-life, so they act only in the cells that produce them or in their immediate envi-
ronment. Their biological effects are, in general, broad and intense. It is important to note, however, that these effects are highly
